extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of American literature; readers studying/critically assessing authors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading and critically evaluating the works of American authors (poets, novelists, short-story writers, dramatists) using focused questions on themes, style, technique, influence, and context. The page provides author-by-author 'Suggestions for Reading' directing comparative, formal, and thematic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read prefaces for theory of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the prefaces to Irradiations and Goblins and Pagodas for Mr. Fletcher's theory of poetry before you read the poems themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From John Gould Fletcher: establish the author's stated theory first so you can judge how successfully the poems realize that theory; specifically ask: Has he succeeded in making the arts of painting and music do service to poetry?

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Aiken's criticism of Fletcher
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the poems, consider the justice or injustice of Mr. Aiken's criticism: 'It is a sort of absolute poetry, a poetry of detached waver and brilliance, a beautiful flowering of language alone--a parthenogenesis, as if language were fertilized by itself rather than by thought or feeling. Remove the magic of phrase and sound and there is nothing left: no thread of continuity, no thought, no story, no emotion. But the magic of phrase and sound is powerful, and it takes one into a fantastic world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the poems to this quoted criticism to judge whether Fletcher's work rests primarily on language/music or also on thought and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify poems that resist Aiken's remark
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find any poems to which the quotation given above does not apply? Are these of more or of less value than the others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After weighing Aiken's critique, classify individual poems as conforming or not, and evaluate relative value accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: List unfamiliar subjects and test truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a list of subjects that you have not found treated elsewhere in poetry. Test the truth of the treatment by your own experience and decide whether Mr. Frost has converted these commonplace experiences into a new field of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Robert Frost: focus on originality of subject matter and whether Frost's treatment elevates common experience into poetic territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authenticity of New England poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Read in succession the poems concerning New England life and decide whether they seem more authentic and more valuable than the others. If so, why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge regional authenticity and its effect on poetic value; look for features that make these poems feel 'authentic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate photographic realism vs artistic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Is Mr. Frost's realism photographic? Consider in this connection his own statement: 'There are two types of realist--the one who offers a good deal of dirt with his potato to show that it is a real one; and the one who is satisfied with the potato brushed clean.... To me the thing that art does for life is to strip it to form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Frost's statement to weigh how much detail he includes and whether that detail serves artfully to 'strip life to form.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze narrative and dramatic strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Read several of the long poems to discover his relative strength in narrative and in dramatic presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare long poems for narrative coherence and dramatic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine vocabulary for naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the vocabulary for naturalness, colloquialism, and extraordinary occasional fitness of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess diction: is language natural and colloquial, and do occasional striking words fit context and purpose?

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarize author's philosophy and attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to sum up briefly Mr. Frost's philosophy of life and his attitude toward nature and people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesize themes and recurring attitudes across poems to articulate Frost's worldview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess metrical forms and musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: What do you observe about the metrical forms, the beauty or lack of beauty in the rhythm? Do many of the poems sing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze meter, rhythm, and musical qualities; note which poems succeed as 'songs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculate on author's future
rubrics_metrics.description: What do you prophesy as to Mr. Frost's future?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on current work, consider likely directions and development in the poet's career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare European and Chicago stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare Mr. Fuller's stories of Europe with his studies of life in Chicago. What is their relative success? What inferences do you draw?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Henry Blake Fuller: assess comparative strengths, themes, and techniques across settings to draw conclusions about the author's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place work in development of American novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering dates, materials, and methods, where do you place Mr. Fuller's work in the development of the American novel?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize Fuller historically: note influences, innovations, and relation to broader novelistic trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference criticism before reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reading On the Stairs, cf. Dial, 64 ('18): 405.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult contemporary criticism/reviews to inform reading of specific works (suggested for Fuller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Read autobiographical books for background
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the autobiographical books, A Son of the Middle Border and A Daughter of the Middle Border, to get the background of Mr. Garland's work. Then read his essays called Crumbling Idols, for the literary theory on which his work was created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Hamlin Garland: establish biographical and theoretical context to better understand themes and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study literary influences and landmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Two literary landmarks in Mr. Garland's history are: Edward Eggleston's The Hoosier Schoolmaster (1871), and Joseph Kirkland's Zury: the Meanest Man in Spring County (1887). Read these and decide how much they influenced Main-Traveled Roads and similar volumes of Mr. Garland's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Garland's works with identified antecedents to trace influence and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek evidence of authentic farm life
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Garland says that he presents farm life 'not as the summer boarder or the young lady novelist sees it--but as the working farmer endures it.' Find evidence of this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for lived detail, perspective, and material conditions that support Garland's claim to authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess dependence on material vs craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how far Mr. Garland's success depends upon the richness of his material, how far upon his philosophy of life and his honesty to his own experience, and how far upon his technical skill as a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the relative contributions of subject-matter, worldview, authenticity, and technique to overall achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify author's limitations and strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: What are his most obvious limitations? What is the relative importance of his novels and of his short stories?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate weaknesses and assess which forms best showcase the author's talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze specific craft elements separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider separately: (1) his power of visualization; (2) his choice of significant detail; (3) his originality or lack of it; (4) his range in characterization; (5) his power of suggestion as over against his vividness of delineation; (6) his economy--or lack of it--in expression. Where does his main strength lie?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down craft into components and judge each to locate primary strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare with Henry James and others
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Gerould belongs to the school of Henry James, but shows marked individuality in her themes and in her dramatic power. A comparison of some of her short stories with stories by Mr. James (q.v.) and by Mrs. Wharton (q.v.) is illuminating for the powers and limitations of all three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Katharine Fullerton Gerould: use comparative reading with James and Wharton to reveal stylistic and thematic affinities or differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare with Katherine Mansfield's Bliss
rubrics_metrics.description: Another interesting comparison is between Mrs. Gerould's stories and the collection entitled Bliss by the English writer, Katherine Mansfield (Mrs. J. Middleton Murry); cf. Manly and Rickert, Contemporary British Literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place Gerould in an international/modernist context by comparing specific collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify social creed and roots
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the main features of the social creed at the root of Giovannitti's poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Arturo Giovannitti: analyze ideological/social commitments informing the poetry (e.g., socialism, labor concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test poet or propagandist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is he a poet or a propagandist? Test his sincerity; his passion; his truth to experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether political/social messaging dominates or is integrated poetically; assess authenticity and artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess limitations as thinker and poet
rubrics_metrics.description: What are his limitations as thinker and as poet?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically weigh intellectual depth and poetic craft to identify shortcomings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare with Whitman in ideas and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare and contrast his work with Whitman's in ideas and in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Whitman as a comparative touchstone for free verse, scope, and democratic themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge presence of greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you find marks of greatness in him?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesize previous analyses to reach a judgment on the author's stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note use of setting and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Note Mr. Hergesheimer's use of setting and atmosphere. What is the relative importance of these to plot and character?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Joseph Hergesheimer: analyze whether atmosphere/setting serve as dominant elements and how they interact with plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess evidences of originality
rubrics_metrics.description: What evidences of originality do you find in his books?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify novel techniques, perspectives, or treatments that distinguish the author's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify as realist or romanticist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the author a realist or a romanticist? Is it true, as has been said, that he stands midway between the 'unrelieved realism' of the new school of writers and the 'genteel moralism' of the old?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the author on a realism–romanticism spectrum and evaluate hybrid tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh criticisms about style and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider these two criticisms of Mr. Hergesheimer's work: (1) He aims to set down 'relative truth ... the colors and scents and emotions of existence'; and (2) he is at times as much concerned 'with the stuffs as with the stuff of life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two cited criticisms to judge balance between sensory/ornamental detail and substantive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study style: suggestion, word choice, rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a special study of his style: (1) of his use of suggestion; (2) of his choice of words; (3) of his feeling for rhythm. Is it true that there is both art and artifice in his methods?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform close stylistic analysis to distinguish genuine artistry from artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge overall contribution to American literature
rubrics_metrics.description: In what ways, if any, has he made actual contribution to American literature? Can you prophesy as to his future?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthesize historical, thematic, and stylistic findings to assess lasting contribution and likely development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place work as social criticism vs character focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Mr. Herrick's work must be regarded as primarily social criticism of American life. Does the interest tend to centre rather upon the problems of the characters, growing out of their circumstances, or upon the characters themselves?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Robert Herrick: determine whether emphasis is on social conditions/problems or on individual characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess scope vs intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is Mr. Herrick's work more notable for scope and breadth or for intensity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare expansiveness of subject matter with concentrated intensity of treatment to characterize style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify poetic qualities in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Note, especially in the novels previous to 1905, the conscientious artistry, the compactness of structure, and the unity of tone commonly associated with poetry. What other qualities characteristic of poetry appear in Mr. Herrick's work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for poetic devices—unity, concision, imagery, musicality—among prose techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare structure of earlier and later works
rubrics_metrics.description: With the structure of his earlier work compare that of the Memoirs of an American Citizen as showing an attempt at greater breadth of canvas and greater variety of tone. Trace this attempt further in his later work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track formal evolution from compact earlier works to broader later canvases; note changes in tone and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for a theory of the art of the novelist
rubrics_metrics.description: What evidences do you find in Mr. Herrick's novels of a carefully wrought theory of the art of the novelist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for explicit or implicit theoretical principles guiding narrative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate characterisation 'discouraged idealist' label
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone has called Mr. Herrick 'a discouraged idealist.' Is this just?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess themes, tone, and worldview to confirm or refute the characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare Harrison with Dickens, Sterne, Meredith
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the article by Robert Herrick listed below, and compare Harrison's work with that of Dickens, Sterne, and Meredith. Deal with each novelist separately according to the influences noted by Mr. Herrick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Henry Sydnor Harrison: perform influence-based comparative reading using a cited critical article as guide.
